newsitem.title: USA: Miami Port gets watchdog after 5 yrs of deficits.
newsitem.headline: Miami Port gets watchdog after 5 yrs of deficits.

text.p: Florida's Dade County manager will appoint a watchdog committee to monitor finances at the Port of Miami, which has run a deficit in each of the last five years, the Miami Herald said Tuesday.
According to a report released at a Monday meeting of the county commission's Maritime Trade Committee, the seaport's general fund budget deficit grew to $22 million this year.

County manager Armando Vidal said he would appoint a monitoring committee, but recommended that the county proceed with a $163 million port expansion project that will add additional cruise ship berths.
The seaport is run by the county and is supposed to be self-supporting, but its shortfalls have been covered with general fund revenues for the last five years, the newspaper said.

The county financed recent expansions at the port using 1992 projections that revenues would rise to $33.2 million this year. But the cruise industry has been flat since 1989 and 1997 revenues are now estimated at only $23.2 million.
Although cruise ships have added new ships, they retired their older ones after a new safety law was passed in 1992, port director Carmen Lunetta told the commissioners.

The port also suffered a $4 million loss when a major cargo company failed, and has been unable to collect nearly $24 million in back payments and interest from the company that manages the port's gantry cranes, Lunetta told the commissioners.
His projections show the port's finances will start turning around this year as a fleet of new cruise ships start to come on line, enabling the port to repay the county general fund.
Assistant County Manager David Morris said county administrators did not realize the extent of the port's shortfalls until this year, when they started to separate and analyze port accounts.
Additionally, Morris said the commissioners themselves had siphoned off millions of dollars from the seaport over the past five years to fund parades, charities, festivals and clubs.
A pending ordinance would halt that practice.

Port financial analysts said taking on new debt would leave the port with a cushion of only about $7 million a year each year until 2015, possibly forcing the seaport to dip into county general funds if revenue projections fall short again.
